Qualia. The subjective, qualitative features of conscious experience—the way things feel or appear to you. The redness of red, the painfulness of pain, the taste of coffee: these are qualia. The philosophical puzzle is how to account for qualia scientifically. If the brain is purely physical and objective, how do subjective qualities of experience arise from it? This explanatory gap between physical processes and subjective properties constitutes one of philosophy of mind's most vexing problems.

Qualia, singular quale, are intrinsically subjective and first-personal. Your experience of red is only knowable directly to you.

The hard problem of consciousness turns largely on qualia: explaining why and how physical brain processes generate subjective experience.

Materialism struggles with qualia. It seems that knowing all physical facts about the brain would not tell you what seeing red is like, what philosophers call the knowledge argument.

The explanatory gap appears to be an unbridgeable gap between objective, third-person brain science and subjective, first-person experience.

Functionalism tries to reduce qualia to functional roles—the property of responding to red in certain ways—but critics argue this misses the subjective feel.

Frank Jackson's knowledge argument poses a case: could a person who knows all physical facts about color still be ignorant of what color looks like?

The inverted spectra thought experiment asks whether your subjective experience of red could be the mirror opposite of mine, yet we both call it red.

The representationalist response argues qualia are not intrinsic properties of experience but representations of external world features.

Illusionists argue qualia as typically conceived do not really exist. What we call qualitative properties are really just ways things seem.

Panpsychism offers one response. If consciousness is fundamental, qualia are not anomalous; they are basic features of reality.

Qualia connect to consciousness, which qualia are the defining feature of, making the mind-body problem acute. They embody the core mystery of the mind-body problem: how subjective properties relate to objective physical facts. Materialism faces the challenge of explaining how purely physical processes generate qualitative experience. Dualism was motivated by qualia when some philosophers posited a separate mental realm to accommodate subjective properties. Qualia are central to contemporary philosophy of mind and cognitive science debates. Panpsychism is one proposed solution: if consciousness is fundamental, qualia are not explanatorily problematic. And Descartes raised questions about the divide between extended body and thinking mind that qualia now sharpen.
